title: 4 Pillars of Cancer Support Doctors Don't Have Time to Teach
guestBio: Jen Miramontes is a Certified Cancer Exercise Specialist and the founder of Cancer Champions, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit that supports cancer patients, survivors, and care partners through four pillars: nutrition, exercise, mindset, and community. Her mission began when she helped her mother — given three months to live — hike in and out of the Grand Canyon and go on to live three more quality years. Cancer Champions is free to join and serves people at any point in a cancer journey.
excerpt: After her mother was given three months to live, Jen Miramontes turned personal loss into a nonprofit mission. In this episode, she breaks down the four pillars oncologists recommend but rarely have time to teach — and what to do in the first week after a cancer diagnosis.
metaDescription: Jen Miramontes of Cancer Champions shares the 4 pillars — nutrition, exercise, mindset, community — that support healing during a cancer journey.
keyTakeaways: Oncologists consistently recommend nutrition, exercise, mindset, and community support, but with only about ten minutes per patient appointment, they rarely have the time to show people how to put those recommendations into practice.

Research now shows that movement during cancer treatment — even a five-minute walk to the end of your street — reduces recurrence rates, improves outcomes, and directly counters the outdated advice to rest and save your energy.

Personalized nutrition matters more than a generic internet search; every cancer and every person is different, and a plan built around your treatment, your side effects, and your food preferences will serve you far better than a one-size-fits-all approach.

A cancer diagnosis can feel profoundly lonely even when friends and family are close by, because the person with cancer is often quietly protecting the people they love by holding back how they really feel.

Reclaiming a sense of personal agency — deciding how support shows up in your life, what foods feel right, what movement you're willing to try — is one of the most powerful things someone navigating cancer can do.

Breathwork, mindset coaching, and community walks are not soft extras; they are evidence-informed practices that reduce pain, lower stress, and keep people motivated enough to stay consistent with the physical pillars.

Cancer Champions is free to join and supports not only the person with cancer but also their care partners, recognizing that the people who love someone through a diagnosis need a place to be held too.

quiz.title: How Do You Move Through Life's Hardest Seasons?
quiz.description: Cancer Champions founder Jen Miramontes built her mission on four pillars — nutrition, exercise, mindset, and community. But the way each of us instinctively moves through difficulty is unique. This quiz explores your natural approach to navigating life's hardest chapters, so you can lean into your strengths and discover where a little extra support might open something new.

A.name: The Steady Nourisher
A.description: When life gets hard, you instinctively turn inward and focus on the fundamentals — what you're eating, how you're sleeping, the small rituals that keep you grounded. You understand that caring for your body is an act of resilience, not indulgence. Your greatest strength is consistency: even in the storm, you keep showing up for yourself in quiet, tangible ways. This episode will affirm everything you're already doing and give you language to share it with someone who needs it.

B.name: The Courageous Mover
B.description: You process life through your body. When the world feels uncertain, movement is your medicine — a walk, a workout, a hike that reminds you what you're capable of. You're the one who shows up even when you're tired, because you've learned that momentum is its own kind of hope. This episode will deepen your understanding of why that instinct is backed by science, and how to carry it into the moments when moving feels hardest.

C.name: The Mindful Witness
C.description: You move through difficulty by getting still. You journal, reflect, breathe, and notice — and you've learned that honoring the full range of your emotions, without forcing positivity, is where real healing lives. You hold space for yourself and for others with unusual grace. This episode will give you practical tools and affirming language for the mindset work you already know matters deeply.

D.name: The Community Anchor
D.description: You don't do hard things alone — and you've discovered that's a superpower, not a weakness. Your first instinct is to reach for connection: a friend, a group, a shared walk, a table where everyone belongs. You know that being witnessed by people who truly understand changes something in a person. This episode will remind you why the community pillar is never soft or secondary, and inspire you to build it even wider.

questions.question: It's the first hard week after receiving unexpected, life-changing news. What do you reach for first?

options.text: The kitchen — I start thinking about what I can cook that will actually make me feel like myself.
My running shoes or gym bag — I need to move before I can think clearly.
My journal or a quiet room — I need to sit with this before I can do anything else.
My phone — I need to hear someone's voice who gets it.

questions.question: A friend tells you they're exhausted and overwhelmed. What's your most natural response?

options.text: I offer to bring them a meal or help them figure out what they need to eat to feel better.
I invite them on a walk — movement almost always helps shift the energy.
I sit down and ask them to tell me everything, without rushing to fix it.
I gather a few people who care about them and create a plan to surround them with support.

questions.question: When you think about the season of life you're in right now, which best describes where you are?

options.text: I'm in a tending season — focused on the basics, keeping things rooted and healthy.
I'm in a moving season — pushing forward, building momentum, not letting anything slow me down.
I'm in a reflecting season — going inward, processing, figuring out what this chapter means.
I'm in a gathering season — investing in people, deepening relationships, building my circle.

questions.question: What does "taking care of yourself" most naturally look like for you on a hard day?

options.text: Making something nourishing to eat, even if it's simple.
Getting outside, even for just a few minutes of movement.
Breathing through it and giving myself permission to feel exactly what I feel.
Calling someone who will just listen without judgment.

questions.question: Jen's mom set an audacious goal — hiking in and out of the Grand Canyon — when she had every reason not to. What does that story stir in you?

options.text: Deep respect for how she kept nourishing and rebuilding her body, one small step at a time.
Total inspiration — I believe movement can unlock things nothing else can.
Awe at her mindset — the decision to believe in possibility when all the data said otherwise.
A reminder that she didn't do it alone — Jen was right there with her, and that made it possible.

questions.question: If you could strengthen one thing about how you move through life's hardest seasons, what would it be?

options.text: Learning to truly nourish myself instead of running on empty when everything gets hard.
Trusting that movement is medicine even when I have no energy left to give.
Making more room for the hard emotions instead of pushing past them too quickly.
Letting people in instead of protecting them from what I'm really going through.

It's really interesting that I don't know why that popped into my mind like I was with a group of moms this morning at Crossline Church talking to them about my new book and a lot of them had the new babies and a lot of them were postpartum and it is that you know getting those those resources are so important for anybody going through a big shift in their life, big changes in life. Life is full of these kinds of things. >> Absolutely. >> Yeah. So you've taken an incredibly difficult personal experience and transformed it into something that serves others. How has building Cancer Champions changed you as a woman and as a leader? >> It's just been remarkable and I think you know as as a woman we're we tend to want to do for others in general anyway, but to have this opportunity to to actually be able to make impact, to make a difference in someone's life, it's an honor that I never would have expected. And then the people the the team that that we have, the individuals that want to come in and help out, it's beautiful. It's just lovely. I feel very fortunate and to to be able to actually do it. Like it it was an idea. There's this idea and there's got to be a way and then to make it happen. I would just say to anyone out there if you feel like if there's just that little thing back there where you're like I just feel like I could make a difference. I just feel like this is something I I want to do, go for it cuz you never know and what you what could come from it is something that impacts hundreds or thousands even. >> So true. I love that. Leading a nonprofit focused on cancer must carry enormous emotional responsibility. How do you personally practice the four pillars that you're teaching others? >> You know, I say it all the time. If I if I don't live it, I can't teach it. That has been a part of my life always, fitness and nutrition primarily. The mindset work is something that came a little later, like really understanding how important that was cuz I was one of those ones that would be very self-deprecating and you realize like that doesn't serve me or the people around me to do that. Like I if I'm saying those things about myself, then that's going to become real. So I'm not going Let's Let's just work on changing our mindset. Breathwork is something I've only learned in the like during this having starting this started this. Community has always been very very important to me. As I was going through this with my mom, these four pillars were part of my life and I thought, well, if if I can impart this to her and then seeing the impact that it had on her, like I said, like blending, you know, healthy foods and moving to see a change immediately in her quality of life was That was so powerful. >> It really it is. You know when it works. It works when it works, right? >> Yes, exactly. [laughter] Exactly. >> And when you look toward the future, what's your biggest dream for Cancer Champions? >> Oh, that's such an easy one for me. My goal is that anyone that hears those words, you have cancer, also hears and we have a resource for you. We have a place you can go that will support you outside of your medical treatment. I just want everyone to know about us. I I mentioned in our luncheon that one of the things that I hear so so often is I wish I would have known about Cancer Champions when and I just don't want that for people. Now we have to figure out how to get into more oncologist office, it sounds like. >> Yes. Yes. Yes, that is you you just hit it. Yeah, you hit that perfect. >> You know, my little business mind gets thinking on things. >> [laughter] >> Clearly. Yes. Yes, I need you on my team. >> I'll be right there. >> I need that business mind. >> [laughter] >> I'll be right there. I know when you were talking about the mindset and the self-deprecation, in my new book The Cultivate Her, I would call those weeds. If you're if your life is a garden and your mind is a garden, it's like we can choose to plant these seeds of like hope, peace, love, kindness towards ourselves, kindness towards others. And then sometimes these like yucky little weeds pop up. And it's like when we have weeds in our soil, they're taking the nutrients from all of the seeds we really want to grow. So it's, you know, that self-deprecation is that weed. It's like, no thanks. And once that's gone, look at how much room it made in your life for this abundance and this spaciousness and this creation of this ability to serve others. When you think about the people you've supported through cancer, what have they taught you about what really matters in life? >> Ah, God, such a good question. Embracing who you are, where you are in that moment. So many of us, myself included, are just constantly looking what's out there. When somebody's going through cancer, they're here. They're present. content:
There is a moment Jen Miramontes will never forget. Her mother had just been told she had three months to live — a terminal diagnosis following years of esophageal cancer treatment. And instead of collapsing under the weight of that news, Jen asked her one question: Is there something we can do to make these next three months your best three months?

Her mother's answer was characteristically audacious. She wanted to hike in and out of the Grand Canyon.

So they got to work. Short walks became longer walks became hikes. Jen blended whole foods to help her mother get nutrients without the chemical-laden shakes. They worked on mindset — not toxic positivity, not forced smiles, but real, grounded hope. And something extraordinary happened. Her mother's quality of life improved. She slept through the night. Her appetite returned. She had energy. She hiked in and out of the Grand Canyon. And she lived three more quality years beyond that terminal diagnosis.

That is the story behind Cancer Champions — and it is the reason this episode of The Manage Her matters so much.

The Gap Between What Doctors Recommend and What They Can Teach

Here is something that might surprise you: oncologists already know that nutrition, exercise, mindset, and community are essential to their patients' outcomes. They are actively recommending all four. The problem is not knowledge — it is time. The average oncologist has about ten minutes per patient. One oncologist on the Cancer Champions board received twelve years of medical education that included approximately fifteen minutes of nutrition training.

That gap — between what the medical world knows patients need and what it has capacity to teach them — is exactly what Cancer Champions was built to fill. Jen is not working around oncologists. She is working alongside them. When she describes doctors saying, "Thank goodness, we finally have a place to send people," you understand why this model is spreading.

What the Four Pillars Actually Look Like in Practice

Jen breaks down each pillar in ways that feel immediately actionable, not overwhelming. Nutrition starts not with a list of forbidden foods but with a question: what does your treatment look like, and what are your side effects? Nausea, appetite loss, weight fluctuation — the plan is built around you, not around whatever the internet decided was the right cancer diet this week. That AI search result does not know you. It does not know how you are going to persevere.

Movement may be the most counterintuitive pillar for anyone who has been told to rest and save their energy. That advice, Jen says plainly, is no longer supported by research. Moving your body — even a five-minute walk to the end of your street and back — reduces recurrence rates, improves outcomes, and brings something that medicine cannot prescribe: the felt experience of agency. This is something I can control. That feeling is not small. When a diagnosis has stripped away so much of your sense of power, reclaiming it through movement is quietly transformative.

Mindset does not mean performing positivity you do not feel. Jen is clear and compassionate about this. People navigating cancer are often quietly protecting the people around them, holding back the full weight of their fear so their family does not have to carry it. Cancer Champions offers coach navigators — mentors who have been through it, who can hold the full truth of what someone is feeling without being emotionally destabilized by it. There is also breathwork: structured, evidence-informed practice that helps people move through fear, manage pain, and stay grounded in what is happening right now.

Community addresses something that often goes unspoken. Even when you are surrounded by people who love you, a cancer diagnosis can feel profoundly lonely — because no one around you is living inside the same experience. Finding people who have been where you are, who can walk alongside you without needing you to protect them, changes something. And notably, Jen says, those community walks and coffee dates do not always center cancer. Sometimes people just talk about the view, their kids, a funny thing that happened. That normalcy is its own kind of medicine.

What to Do First

If you or someone you love has just received a diagnosis, Jen offers three starting points. First, take a deep breath — a real one, slow and deliberate. Second, step away from the internet, or at minimum, hold what you find there very lightly, because it does not know you. Third, go to cancerchampions.org and join. It is free. You fill out a simple form and a real support structure meets you on the other side.

She also offers one small step for each pillar you can take this week. For nutrition, ask yourself how you can best nourish your body — not what you have to cut out, but what you can add. For movement, walk to the end of your street. That is it. For mindset, take one deep breath from the diaphragm, hold it, exhale, and let yourself picture the other side of this. For community, let one person in. Let someone bring you food, give you a ride, sit with you. The people who love you want to do something. Letting them is a gift to both of you.

The Leader Behind the Mission

Jen Miramontes practices every pillar she teaches — not as a performance of wellness, but because she learned firsthand that it works. The mindset work came later for her than the physical pillars did. She describes being self-deprecating for years before realizing that the story she told about herself was becoming real, and deciding she was done letting those weeds grow. That metaphor resonated deeply with Aimee, who explores the same idea in her newest book, The Cultivate Her: your mind is a garden, and what you choose to tend determines what has room to flourish.

When Aimee asked Jen what people navigating cancer have taught her about what really matters, her answer was simple and worth sitting with: They are here. They are present. They are all about what is happening right now. Not the future, not the past — this moment, today, the best day they can make of it.

That is not just a lesson for cancer. That is a lesson for all of us. And it is the kind of wisdom that only comes from the people who have had to learn it in the most honest, unguarded way possible.

Visit cancerchampions.org to learn more, join the community, or find out how you can volunteer or donate. There is no cost to become a champion.

This conversation shares personal experience and general wellness education. It is not medical advice. Please talk with your oncology team before making any changes to your nutrition or exercise during treatment.
